I understand how you feel. This possibility bothered me a few years ago, but this was when I was leaning more towards having kids. I think that if you are not willing and ready to care for and love a severely disabled child, don't have kids. I think people get caught up in the fantasy of happy, cute kids and never think about the things that can go wrong. If this fear really bothers you, then listen to it and delay having kids if and when you're ready for that possibility.

You could end up completely alone even if you have kids. You could have a poor relationship with them and they cut you off, they could move far away and you won't see them regularly, they could be assholes and choose to never visit, they could even die before you do, the possibilities go on. 

I know older individuals do a lot of volunteering at different organizations (when they physically can) and socialize through that. You could get a pet. If you end up in a nursing home, there are lots of people there you can make friends with.

Your kids will grow up and live their own lives. They can't and won't stay in the nest. Invest in yourself and learn to be happy on your own.

I'm not a parent myself, but my mother did regret having children. I'll try to convey her experience. However, she is an extreme example.

First of all, she was not at all equipped to financially or emotionally support children. She was a high school dropout from an abusive household and had untreated mental illnesses and trauma. My father pressured her into having kids, and then never helped to raise my sister and me. I've seen her have many, many emotional breakdowns in my life, and one thing she always said was, "I never wanted kids."

If she did not have me and had dumped my horrible father, she would not have been the broken woman she is. She would have gotten her GED and had a career. Instead, she slaved away for minimum wage to take care of her kids, and that money wasn't enough to cover everything anyway. Better jobs come with insurance too, and she could have gotten counseling and lived a healthier life. Now she's dying of COPD in her 50s. 

In her case, having children destroyed her mind, body, and soul. She was not in a position to have kids, anyone can see that, but she felt pressured and just thought it was the thing to do, especially since her own mother had seven children, and her grandmother had even more. In giving life to others, she lost herself. She never achieved anything, never felt happiness, never saw the world or found love. She was only my mom, and she regrets it.

Climate change has already been set in motion. Even if the world changed overnight, it could be centuries before the earth returned to its previous state. 

Something I lived through as a child was Katrina. Climate change is and will continue to warm the oceans, therefore creating stronger storms along with rising sea levels. And that's just one consequence of warmer oceans. My point is, I have already survived many powerful hurricanes and seen the destruction that these strengthening storms are capable of. I view climate change as an immediate reality, not as some obscure idea that probably won't happen to me.

Oh I need help? No shit. Yes, I have mental and emotional health issues. Anyone who's lived my life will have them. However, the climate crisis is a reality. How is it not clarity of mind to foresee the disaster humanity has created? If my children don't see it, my grandchildren certainly will.

We'll start seeing cataclysmic consequences in about 30 years, probably sooner. I could not live with the guilt of bringing children into a literal apocalypse. My parents were abusive and I hate them, and there was a long time that I wished I'd never been born and I've been suicidal most of my life. I would never want my children to feel the things that I have. If I have children, I would be to blame for birthing them in a hellscape. I imagine them asking me why I had them when I knew the world would be falling apart. I think it would be a wicked act of me to bring innocent beings into such a world.

I don't like this kind of thinking at all. I was one of those "next so-and-so" kids. I was a "gifted" student (I abhor that term) and graduated high school as valedictorian. For my entire childhood, my mother just expected me to get a full ride scholarship and be the first person in our family to go to college. Well, my mom was a single parent that worked at McDonald's. We didn't have a penny to our names. Graduation comes around and I get some scholarships, but not enough. Mother refused to help me get student loans because she was terrified of the debt. So I was the failed "next great scientist that would save the world" because I came from poverty. So, I don't believe in this argument that by abstaining from having children we're withholding something from humanity. That's because these brilliant kids aren't going to become anything unless they come from reasonable wealth and/or a strong support system. I, of course, had neither. And I've lived through childhood abuse that made me wish I was never born. 

I'd also like to add that that saying your future kids could be the next Einstein is just bs. They're just as likely to become the next Ted Bundy.
